problem: Zero-shot object goal navigation methods guide exploration with categorical semantic maps that treat objects as monolithic entities. They fail when the target is only partially observed and they lack functional/detail cues; single-scale CLIP similarity also misses small parts.
motivation: Humans find objects in unfamiliar places by first spotting distinctive geometric parts (e.g. a chair back) and by reasoning about function. Categorical maps discard these fine-grained and functional cues, so the agent passes by targets that are only partly visible.
key_idea: Build a 2D map of multi-scale CLIP similarity scores between observations and LLM-generated geometric-part and affordance attributes of the target, and explore the highest-scoring frontier area.
insight: Part and affordance attributes give a denser, more robust exploration signal than the category name. In the Na/Ng ablation (Fig. 3 / Table 6), geometric parts contribute more than affordances, and using both is best. Multi-scale patches help small parts (SR +~10%, SPL +~20% from 1 to 4 levels), and max-pooled map updating beats average or replacement. Table 4 shows lower detection, planning and exploration errors than categorical guidance.
method: Attribute generation: GPT-4V is prompted to produce Na affordance attributes and Ng geometric-part visual features for the target object (Na=1, Ng=3 in the main experiments).

Multi-scale attribute scoring: the RGB image is split into 4^(k-1) equal patches at each level (3 levels: 1, 4, 16 patches), each patch is resized and encoded by CLIP, and cosine similarity to each attribute text embedding is computed. Per-pixel scores are averaged across levels.

GAMap construction: depth is back-projected into a point cloud, transformed to the world frame and projected to a ground-plane grid with C=Na+Ng channels. Cells keep the max score over points, and are updated across time steps by max with the previous value.
Exploration policy: frontier areas are ranked by the GA score averaged over attribute channels, and the highest-scoring one is chosen as the goal.
Local planning: the Fast Marching Method plans the shortest path to the chosen area and produces low-level actions, repeated with map updates until the target is reached or the episode ends.

setting.backbone: CLIP (frozen visual and text encoders) + GPT-4V (frozen, attribute generation only); no learned policy, FMM planner
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions along an FMM path to a frontier goal; STOP
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D and Gibson scenes); real-world tests on a JetAuto-Pro robot
setting.privileged: none (assumes perfect RGB-D calibration and given pose)

numbers.eval_set_note: 2000 episodes on the HM3D validation split, following L3MVN protocol
numbers.extra: 3 scale levels, Na=1, Ng=3; FMM planner, no trained locomotion or semantic module
3 scale levels, Na=1, Ng=3; FMM planner

numbers_note: Ablations use the official mini-validation split of HM3D, with different numbers (e.g. SR 50.25). They are reported in Tables 2, 3 and 6 and are not included as entries.
results: GAMap reaches SR 53.1 / SPL 26.0 on HM3D and SR 85.7 / SPL 55.5 on Gibson. It beats VLFM's value map + FMM (50.9/23.6 on HM3D, 82.8/48.5 on Gibson) and VoroNav on HM3D. VLFM with its trained policy has a higher SPL on HM3D (30.4).
limitations: Depends on the CLIP scoring quality and on the correctness of LLM-inferred attributes.
Multi-scale scoring and multiple attributes add computation (about 2 FPS, and time grows with Na, Ng and scales).
Assumes perfect calibration and pose; a real-world evaluation is only described qualitatively, with no numbers.
